acceptable.choice: Flask (which the research software engineer already knows) with a small HTML upload form, plus a background job queue on the existing VM
acceptable.why: It uses the team's current skills, and the CPU need is tiny: a few dozen runs of at most 90 seconds is roughly one CPU-hour a day, which 4 vCPUs handle easily with 2–3 workers.

acceptable.choice: RQ + Redis, or Huey (Redis- or SQLite-backed) as the job queue
acceptable.why: These are the simplest Python task queues that keep 20–90 second runs out of the web request, and they have very few parts to maintain.

acceptable.choice: A job table in SQLite or plain files, with a worker managed by systemd that runs jobs through a ProcessPoolExecutor or subprocess
acceptable.why: At this load, a database-backed queue with no extra infrastructure is enough and is the least work to keep running.

acceptable.choice: FastAPI or Django instead of Flask
acceptable.why: Either is a fine Python choice; Django's built-in admin and user accounts can help, but neither is needed, and Flask keeps the advantage of being familiar.
It works and is well documented, but it has more moving parts and configuration than this load needs; acceptable, not preferred.

acceptable.choice: Gradio with its built-in queue and a concurrency limit, behind authentication
acceptable.why: Pure Python, almost no web code, and its queueing handles long jobs; good for a quick start, though storing results and an audit trail take extra work.

acceptable.choice: Have the web app submit Slurm jobs to the HPC cluster through a service account
acceptable.why: Only acceptable if cluster policy allows automated submission from the VM; it adds queue waits and failure points that this load doesn't need.

acceptable.choice: Package the simulation as a versioned container (Apptainer/Docker) or a pip/conda package with a command-line tool, so collaborators can run it on their own HPC
acceptable.why: Very good for reproducibility and needs no service upkeep; it can sit alongside the web service or replace it if the collaborators have compute and skills.

acceptable.choice: Run the app with Docker Compose or systemd, behind gunicorn and nginx/Caddy with HTTPS
acceptable.why: A standard setup on one VM that rarely needs attention between grants.

acceptable.choice: Wrap the tool for an existing Galaxy server (institutional or usegalaxy.*)
acceptable.why: Reasonable if a Galaxy server the collaborators already use will host it, because someone else does the upkeep; hosting their own Galaxy is not reasonable.

ruled_out.choice: Writing the web layer in Go, Rust, Node.js, Java or another 'faster' language
ruled_out.why: The web layer only takes uploads and serves results, so speed there doesn't matter; a new language breaks the team's skills and doubles what they have to maintain.

ruled_out.choice: Rewriting the simulation in a faster language in order to put it online
ruled_out.why: 20–90 seconds a run is fine for asynchronous jobs at this volume; speeding up the simulation is a separate decision and doesn't block going online (they already have C++ for hot loops).

ruled_out.choice: Running the simulation inside the HTTP request handler
ruled_out.why: 60–90 second requests hit proxy and worker timeouts, tie up the server, and lose the work when the browser disconnects.
Far more operations work than one VM, about 20 users and a lab with little time for upkeep can carry.

ruled_out.choice: Moving to a commercial cloud (AWS Batch/Lambda, GCP, etc.)
ruled_out.why: Adds billing, accounts, data-governance questions and upkeep, when the university VM already has more than enough capacity.

ruled_out.choice: A React/Vue single-page app front end
ruled_out.why: A server-rendered upload form with a status page does the job; a JavaScript build chain is a new skill to learn and more to maintain.

ruled_out.choice: Running a web server on the HPC login nodes
ruled_out.why: Usually against cluster policy, and login nodes are not built to host services.

ruled_out.choice: A shared JupyterHub, or giving collaborators notebooks on the VM
ruled_out.why: Lets collaborators run arbitrary code on the lab VM, is heavy to maintain and secure, and makes results less reproducible than a fixed pipeline.
Takes researcher time for every run and doesn't reliably record which code and parameters produced each result.

must_mention: Answer the question directly: no, they don't need a faster language. The web part is light glue code and Python is plenty; the time goes into the simulation, which runs the same wherever it is called from.
Use an asynchronous job pattern: submit, get a job ID, check status (or get an email), download results. Never run the simulation inside the request.

Capacity estimate: a few dozen runs × 20–90 seconds is about an hour of CPU a day, so the 4 vCPU / 16 GB VM is enough. Cap workers at 2–3 so the web server stays responsive and memory stays within 16 GB.
Limit NumPy/BLAS threads per worker (OMP_NUM_THREADS / OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS) so workers running at the same time don't oversubscribe the 4 vCPUs.
Reproducibility: pin the environment (lockfile or container image), and store with every result the code version (git commit or image tag), the input file, all parameters and the random seed.
Access control: collaborators only, through university SSO / federated login if available, or simple per-user accounts or tokens; HTTPS required.
Check uploads: allowed formats, size limits, parameter ranges, and a per-job timeout. Never unpickle or execute anything a user uploads.
Keep it small and low-maintenance: reuse the existing Python simulation code unchanged as a function or command the worker calls, deploy with Docker Compose or systemd, and write a short runbook.
Plan where results are stored, how long they are kept, and how they are backed up, so jobs aren't lost on restart.
red_flags: Telling them to learn Go, Rust, Node or another language for the web part, or saying Python is too slow for serving
Running the 20–90 second simulation synchronously inside a web request, or using the Flask development server in production
Recommending Kubernetes, microservices, a service mesh or a multi-cloud setup for about 20 users
A public endpoint with no authentication that accepts arbitrary uploads, or one that runs user-supplied code or pickles
Leaving out reproducibility (no environment pinning, no record of code version, parameters or seed with results)
Assuming the web app can freely submit to the HPC cluster without checking cluster policy
Letting unlimited workers or BLAS threads run at once on the VM, which leads to memory exhaustion or CPU thrashing
Proposing a large, multi-month custom platform build that the lab can't maintain between grants
Sending unpublished research data to third-party hosting (e.g. public Hugging Face Spaces) without considering data sensitivity
unknowns: Peak memory per run, and whether a run is single-threaded or uses several cores through BLAS; this decides the safe worker count
How input size affects runtime, and whether any inputs could run much longer than 90 seconds (sets timeouts and limits)
Whether HPC policy allows automated or service-account job submission from the VM
What authentication the university can offer external collaborators (SSO federation such as eduGAIN/InCommon, guest accounts)
University IT rules on exposing the VM to the internet, TLS certificates, firewalls and backups
Whether collaborator inputs or results are sensitive or unpublished, which affects storage, retention and where it may be hosted
Whether the simulation is deterministic given a seed and fixed library versions
Whether collaborators would rather run a container on their own clusters than use a hosted service
Expected growth in users or runs once the service exists
